title: 2026-02-17-gpu-memory-fragmentation-backpressure-troubleshoot-lyra-finance

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-17
Start 15:30 UTC | Duration ~62 minutes | Auto transcript
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Nate Gomez (Redwood SRE), Marcus Lee (Lyra Infra), Sofia Alvarez (Lyra ML), Diane Park (Lyra Head Platform), Jamal Ortiz (Lyra DevOps)

Auto-summary: intermittent OOMs under 99th-percentile load; unusual memory growth and fragmentation after long-running batches; occasional host-device stalls causing request timeouts.

[00:00] Alex (AE): okay hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll jump straight in, Priya and Nate from our side will lead the tech triage. Marcus, do you want to give a 2 minute recap of what you're seeing?
[00:22] Marcus (Infra): yeah thanks Alex. So we've got a handful of incidents over the last two weeks where one of our private nodes goes into hard OOM during sustained traffic bursts around 40rps. It usually starts after long sequences of high token generation — the VM stays up, GPUs show allocated memory but total free GPU memory decreases even though active workloads are low, like fragmentation maybe? Then processes crash or the runtime returns CUDA out of memory.
[00:46] Sofia (ML): to add, model sharding didn't fully help; we tried lowering batch size and pinning model to 8-bit quantized variant — still hit residual failures. The failures seem non-deterministic and sometimes recover after a node restart.
[01:05] Priya (SE): okay good context. A couple quick framing points: we often see two different classes — immediate large allocations that exceed capacity (classic OOM) versus slow fragmentation where allocator can't find contiguous chunk, so repeated allocations fail even though aggregate free memory should be enough. Which pattern aligns with you?
[01:30] Marcus: it looks like fragmentation — nvidia-smi shows 90% memory but tools show a lot of small free pockets. We also saw spikes in h2d latencies around the same time.
[01:45] Nate (SRE): we captured some nvml counters and host cpu queuing, I'll share gists; there were also longer PCIe copy times and NVLink queues backing up — possibly backpressure.
[02:02] Alex: good, let's walk through possible root causes and then debugging steps.

Topic: allocator and fragmentation
[02:15] Priya: the runtime uses a mixed allocator: primary caching allocator on device plus cudaMalloc fallback. Over time, fragmentation can happen if lifetimes vary, small allocations persist, and caching bins become suboptimal. On some driver versions the caching allocator's defrag heuristics are conservative.
[02:40] Sofia: are you referring to the PyTorch cuda caching allocator or a custom one? We run an ONNX-flavored runtime compiled with a custom allocator shim.
[02:50] Priya: right, we saw a couple custom runtimes that implement a pooling layer on top of cudaMalloc — they sometimes forget to coalesce freed segments or reuse pinned host buffers, leading to external fragmentation. The shim could misreport free segments which trips higher-level placement logic.
[03:10] Jamal (DevOps): and we run in a multi-tenant node with k8s device plugin — pods share GPU via MIG slicing on some nodes and full GPU on others, could that mix cause fragmentation?
[03:25] Priya: yep, mixing MIG and full-GPU can produce non-uniform physical layouts and interfere with allocator assumptions; also if there are noisy neighbors doing cudaMalloc/cudaFree frequently, the aggregate effect is higher fragmentation.

Topic: host->device transfer backpressure
[03:40] Priya: another angle is backpressure on host-device transfers. If the host freezes large pinned buffers, PCIe/NVLink queues get congested and the runtime stalls waiting for memcpy to complete, which can cascade into longer-lived allocations and pinned pages leaking.
[04:00] Marcus: that matches: we see elevated host CPU utilization and nvprof shows long memcpy times when these incidents happen. Sometimes a request will hang for 5-10s before timing out.
[04:15] Alex: that explains the timeout symptoms. What about CUDA errors? Which specific error strings in logs?
[04:22] Nate: logs show CUDA error 2 (out of memory) and occasionally CUDA error 700 (launch failure) around the same window; stack traces are noisy because we run released runtime with stripped symbols.
[04:37] Priya: launch failure often follows OOMs when kernel queues get desynced. Good to collect full NVTX ranges and driver logs.

Debugging checklist discussed
[04:50] Priya: here's a checklist we recommend: (1) enable allocator debug traces (dump bins and free lists every 5 minutes), (2) enable nvml and nvprof / Nsight compute traces on suspect host, (3) run a fragmentation stress harness that repeatedly allocates/frees variable sized tensors to reproduce slowly, (4) try per-request soft memory cap and graceful reject path to avoid hard OOMs.
[05:18] Sofia: can you share the stress harness?
[05:21] Priya: yes, we'll send a lightweight Python harness that mimics your batch size distribution and token lengths. It has toggles for pinned vs pageable host buffers, and can run with MIG and non-MIG configs.
[05:35] Alex: also we'll share recommended kernel/driver versions — sometimes upgrades include allocator fixes. Which driver version are you on?
[05:42] Marcus: 535.86.05 on most nodes, a few on 520-era drivers.
[05:48] Priya: 535 has some improvements but also new behavior in unified memory; we'll include notes.

Interruption / transcription noise
[05:55] Speaker 1: uh-huh (inaudible)
[06:00] Priya: sorry can you repeat?
[06:02] Marcus: no, just saying we also saw an odd regression after a security patch that changed kernel iommu settings.
[06:12] Nate: I can correlate that to host PCIe replay counters.

Investigation details and observations
[06:20] Priya: quick note on batching: if you have dynamic batching that accumulates requests into bigger tensors, a single large allocation can momentarily require contiguous memory that isn't available because small stranded allocations fill space. So batching heuristics that create big tensors but free sub-chunks slowly are risky.
[06:44] Sofia: we do a dynamic batcher that builds up to 32 sequences. We tried capping to 8 but still saw fragmentation over long runs.
[06:52] Priya: try two approaches in parallel: a) limit max batch size and enforce preemption (drop to smaller batch if fragmentation counters exceed threshold), b) use chunked generation where large allocations are split into multiple smaller kernels to reduce contiguous allocation pressure.
[07:10] Alex: can Redwood runtime do chunked token generation automatically?
[07:14] Priya: the runtime supports tokenwise chunking and KV cache lazy growth but it needs config toggles; we can provide a safe config that restricts the allocator to smaller max-chunk size.

On quantization and memory footprint
[07:28] Sofia: we tried int8 quantized model and still hit failures. Is quantization not helping fragmentation?
[07:35] Priya: quant reduces per-parameter memory but doesn't help fragmentation of intermediate activation buffers if your runtime uses large scratch buffers. Also some quant kernels allocate ephemeral workspace which can be as large as fp16 kernels. Worth profiling specific operator workspaces.
[07:52] Marcus: are there known kernels with large workspace needs?
[07:55] Priya: some fused attention kernels and cuda graph warm-ups can allocate big temporary buffers; the driver reports these as device allocations that contribute to fragmentation.

Retries and graceful degradation
[08:08] Priya: about retry semantics — we advise a soft-fail path: if allocation fails, instead of immediate crash, return a 503 with a Retry-After and optionally route to smaller model variant or a CPU fallback for short outputs. Hard retries that keep reattempting full-size allocations without backoff worsen fragmentation.
[08:30] Alex: good point. Lyra, what's your current retry logic?
[08:34] Marcus: our app retries twice with exponential backoff but immediately requeues identical workload.
[08:40] Priya: switch to a progressive degradation: on first failure try smaller batch / reduce max tokens / route to quantized variant, and on repeated failures return a controlled degraded response. We'll share a policy template.

Data collection for reproduction
[08:55] Nate: I'll attach nvml timelines, pci counters, and kdump of host memory maps. We also have systemd logs showing oom-killer didn't fire — GPU OOMs only.
[09:05] Priya: request that you also capture process-level malloc traces and runtime NVTX spans. If possible, run with environment variable REDWOOD_ALLOCATOR_DEBUG=1 (we'll provide exact flag) which prints out free list sizes periodically.
[09:20] Marcus: ok we'll enable that for the repro window.

Mid-call interruption and tangents (natural speech)
[09:30] Diane (Head Platform): quick question — if we schedule a repro window on a private node, is there risk of data leakage when running profiler?
[09:38] Alex: instrumentations we ask for are metadata-only and nvprof traces; we have a safe mode for private clusters that avoids payload capture. We'll provide exact commands and a checklist for safe collection.
[09:50] Diane: good. We need an audit trail for this.

Deep technical suggestions
[09:55] Priya: technical suggestions summary: (1) enable allocator debug and gather free-list histograms, (2) test a low-risk driver upgrade on a canary node, (3) enforce per-request soft memory cap and a graceful degrade route, (4) enable periodic defrag sweep in runtime (we have a patch to coalesce small free segments that we can trial), (5) tune batching to reduce single large allocation spikes.
[10:22] Marcus: can we get the defrag patch? We run on-prem and prefer to test changes with your guidance.
[10:29] Priya: yes we'll send a build with the defrag heuristic toggled off by default; you'll run it in the repro window.

Specific log excerpts (verbatim-ish)
[10:40] Marcus: log snippet: "Runtime: cuda error 2 at device_allocator.c:412 - failed to allocate 1.2GiB" then 30s later "cuda error 700 launch failure at kernel.cu:88". Another line: "nvlink: pci replay 12".
[10:58] Priya: useful. The pattern 2 then 700 aligns with fragmentation causing allocation failure then subsequent kernel launch failing due to prior bad state.

Discussion about on-prem/VPC networking and maintenance
[11:10] Diane: our private deployment has strict maintenance windows; can Redwood propose a minimal-impact repro plan?
[11:18] Alex: yes, propose 3-hour window in off-peak, only one node at a time, and we'll provide scripts that produce low-data-noise traces.
[11:26] Jamal: we need an internal approval; we'll aim for next Tue.

Long tail effects and mitigations
[11:35] Priya: longer-term options: enable allocator cross-defrag sweeps nightly, add background compaction job when node idle, adopt a specialized allocator tuned for variable-sized tensor workloads (we can trial tcmalloc-like strategies but on GPU) — that requires engineering time.
[11:55] Sofia: what's the risk of background compaction causing perf regressions?
[12:00] Priya: if compaction runs during high load it can cause stall; do it during idle windows or low priority. We can also throttle compaction threads.

Recap and explicit next steps (closing)
[12:12] Alex: quick recap — we will: 1) Priya send allocator debug flags + harness, 2) Alex propose per-request cap config and retry policy, 3) Marcus run harness and upload traces, 4) schedule repro window for Tue 2026-02-24. Any missing?
[12:30] Marcus: no that covers it. We'll aim to get logs before the repro so you can look.
[12:36] Diane: please include the safe data collection checklist.
[12:40] Priya: yes. We'll also include a suggested A/B test for the defrag patch.
[12:44] Alex: thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with links and the next steps.
[12:50] End meeting.
